title: Lot Depth From Area and Width
description: Find a rectangular lot's depth from its area and width with Lot Depth From Area and Width — area ÷ width, with acre and square-foot inputs. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a quarter-acre lot (10,890 sq ft) with a 66-foot frontage runs 165 feet deep — the classic American building lot, recovered from two numbers on the listing.
quick_answer: Lot Depth From Area and Width finds the missing side of a rectangular lot: depth equals area divided by width. Enter the area and its width and read the depth — the dimension listings omit and fence plans cannot proceed without.
steps_intro: A rectangle has four numbers; any two of area, width and depth give the third:

Front and rear setbacks subtract from depth; knowing the true depth is step one of knowing what house fits — before the architect's meter starts running.
Stated area, width and depth should multiply out. When they don't, someone rounded — or erred — and this page finds which number is the stranger.
66 ft wide × 165 ft deep = 10,890 sq ft = exactly 0.25 acre. The 66-foot frontage (four rods, one chain — surveying's old units) still echoes through American subdivision plats.
Half an acre is 21,780 sq ft; at 110 ft of width the depth is 198 ft. Entering acres directly spares the manual 43,560 multiplication the calculator does for you.

faq: What if my lot is not rectangular?
Then 'depth' is an average, not a side. For irregular parcels, measure the actual shape in the Map Area Calculator and treat this page's answer as a planning approximation only.
Frontage or rear width — which width?
The side you have. For a true rectangle both are equal; for a tapered lot, entering the average width gives the average depth, labelled as such in honest notes.
Yes — acres, square feet and square metres are all accepted; the conversion to a single unit happens inside.
217.8 ft is exact enough for fences and forms; surveys carry depths to hundredths. Round for the lumber order, never for the legal description.
Corner lots wear two frontages — 'width' and 'depth' swap depending on the addressing street. Compute both ways if the plat is ambiguous; zoning usually names the front.
Beyond about 3:1 depth-to-width, lots feel like bowling lanes and price accordingly — the ratio your computed depth reveals is itself market information.
Deed dimensions are horizontal (plan) distances. A steep lot's surface is longer than its plan depth — walkers notice, documents don't.
